known_for: Preacher at Antioch and bishop of Constantinople, who spoke plainly about wealth and the poor and died in exile.

key_works.title: Homilies on Matthew
key_works.about: verse-by-verse sermons, including Homily 50 on honoring Christ in the poor

key_works.title: Homilies on the Statues
key_works.about: twenty-one sermons from the weeks of fear in Antioch in 387

key_works.title: On the Priesthood
key_works.about: written, Socrates says, while he was a deacon at Antioch

legacy_traces: Socrates says his sermons reached readers two ways: some John published himself, and others were taken down in shorthand as he spoke.
Palladius, a bishop who stood by him, wrote a dialogue on his life and fall, and tells the journey into exile.

After his deposition John's followers, called Johannites by their opponents, left the church and held their own services in the public baths and elsewhere. They came back, Socrates says, only when Proclus brought John's body home on the twenty-seventh of January, 438, and laid it in the Church of the Apostles.
legacy_remembered: Honored by Palladius, who defends him throughout his dialogue, and by the crowds who kept watch all night to stop his removal from the church.

Disputed in his lifetime: Severian preached that John's haughtiness was reason enough to depose him, and Sisinnius, the Novatian bishop, wrote against John's saying 'Approach, although you may have repented a thousand times.' Socrates, who tells of both, writes that John's zeal for strictness sat oddly with that sermon.
Socrates notes that Theophilus's condemnation of Origen came about two hundred years after Origen's death, while John was restored to communion in the thirty-fifth year after his deposition.
uncertain: Socrates reports that the sermon over Eutropius struck some as cruel. In the sermon itself John says he was blamed for taking Eutropius into the sanctuary, and that he described the man's fall to move the people to mercy. Socrates also passes on that John was said to be stern and severe, and that a friend of his youth found him more prone to irritability than to modesty.

John ate alone, and Socrates says no one knew why for certain. Palladius, who knew him, says he drank no wine, had a disordered stomach, and sometimes put off his meals while absorbed in prayer and study. Socrates also says people gave other reasons, and that the habit helped his enemies.
Socrates says John died in Comana. Palladius says the soldiers lodged him at a martyr's shrine five or six miles outside the town and that he died there.
